references.text: The original Passover ordinance was given in Egypt, where the fourteenth day of the first month was set as the time for celebrating Passover, which is fulfilled here in the wilderness of Sinai.
Specifically, the time 'between the two evenings' (bein ha'arbayim) is mentioned for the slaughter of the Passover lamb, the same expression used in Numbers 9:5.
The Lord set Passover for the fourteenth day of the first month at evening, as a perpetual feast for Israel.
The tabernacle was erected on the first day of the first month in the second year, shortly before this Passover celebration took place.
The context of Numbers places this Passover celebration in the wilderness of Sinai in the second year after the exodus from Egypt.
Moses repeats the Passover command in the plains of Moab and confirms that Israel shall keep Passover in the month they came out of Egypt.
Israel celebrated Passover at Gilgal on the fourteenth day of the first month, after they had entered the land of Canaan.
King Hezekiah restored the Passover celebration and sent word to all Israel to come to Jerusalem to celebrate Passover.
King Josiah kept Passover for the Lord in Jerusalem, and the Passover lamb was slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the first month.
Paul refers to Christ as our Passover lamb who has been sacrificed, linking the Old Testament Passover ordinance to Christ's atoning work.
